title: ‘am bashtighil — the present tense
goal: Build present-tense verbs for all eight persons, and tell habits from actions in progress with a single word: عَم.
bekal: attach the b- prefix to verbs for all eight persons
tell "I drink coffee every day" from "I'm drinking coffee"
negate a verb with مَا in the right place

dialogs.title: حَكِي — عَ التِّلِفُون
dialogs.intro: Laila calls Budi around midday. Budi is in the campus library.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Grammar. I study two hours every day.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.text: وَاللَّه؟ شَاطِر. أَنَا مَا بِدْرُس هَيْك.
lines.baca: walla? shaaṭir. ana ma bidrus hēk.
lines.id: Really? You're so diligent. I don't study that much.
lines.literal: by-God? clever. I not I-study like-this.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.text: عَم بِسْتَنَّى الْبَاص. رَايْحَة عَ الْبَيْت.
lines.id: Waiting for the bus. I'm going home.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: When do you usually get there?

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.text: بُوصَل قَبِل الْمَغْرِب. بَسّ الْيَوْم فِي زَحْمِة.
lines.baca: buuṣal ’abl el-maghrib. bass el-yōm fi zahme.
lines.id: I get there before sunset. But today there's traffic.
lines.literal: I-arrive before sunset. but today there-is crowding.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Hang in there. I walk home.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Rarely. I like walking, the weather's nice.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: OK, see you tomorrow in class.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّه. سَلِّمِي عَ الْعِيلِة.
lines.id: God willing. Say hi to your family.
lines.literal: if God wills. give-greetings to the-family.

notes: **The b- prefix is required, and this is a big difference from Fusha.** In Fusha "I study" is أَدْرُس; in the Levant it's بِدْرُس *bidrus*, with a b in front. A verb without b only appears after بَدِّي، رَح، لَازِم، مُمْكِن — it never stands alone.

**The word عَم turns a habit into "-ing".** The form بِدْرُس means "I study" as a habit or a general fact. The form عَم بِدْرُس means "I'm studying" right now. It works almost exactly like the English "-ing", which makes this one of the easiest points in the whole book.
**The word عَم never changes form** for any of the eight persons. It's one frozen word you simply put in front. Only the verb after it changes.
**The verb negative is always مَا, and it goes in front of everything.** The forms are مَا بِدْرُس ("I don't study") and مَا عَم بِدْرُس ("I'm not studying"). Never use مِش here.

**The phrase رَايْحَة عَ الْبَيْت uses a participle, not a verb.** The word رَايِح means "going, on the way", and it very often replaces a verb for actions in progress or already decided. The feminine is رَايْحَة and the plural رَايْحِين.

**Sending greetings is part of closing a conversation.** The phrase سَلِّم عَ الْعِيلِة (to a man) or سَلِّمِي (to a woman) almost always comes up, and the answer is بْيِسَلْمُوا ("they send greetings back") even before you've had a chance to pass them on.

grammars.title: Present-tense verbs: two basic patterns
body: The prefix pattern is the same for every verb; only the vowel inside the stem differs. Learn these two verbs as models, and all other verbs follow the same shape.
after: ⚠️ The forms for **you (f)** and **she** are not the same: بْتِدْرْسِي ends in ـِي, while بْتِدْرُس doesn't. And the form for **she** is exactly the same as **you (m)** — that's not a typo, it really is so. Context tells them apart, and it never causes confusion in real conversation.
The **we** form is the only one that doesn't use b- but **mn-**: مْنِدْرُس. Think of it as b- in disguise; the pattern stays the same.

grammars.title: Habits, actions in progress, and their negatives
after: The last two rows show the participle, which for some verbs means a state that **has happened and still holds** — like "have eaten", "have drunk", "know". For verbs of motion such as رَاح and إِجَا, it means "on the way".
At A1 you only need to recognize this form when you hear it and learn the four most common: رَايِح (going), جَايِ (coming), سَاكِن (living), عَارِف (knowing).

blocks.text: Notice the word أَبَدًا, which only works together with a negative: مَا بِشْرَب أَبَدًا. On its own it doesn't mean "never", so don't answer a question with just أَبَدًا — answer with لَا، أَبَدًا.

blocks.title: Time words can go almost anywhere
items: At the start of the sentence: دَايْمًا بِشْرَب قَهْوِة. At the end: بِشْرَب قَهْوِة دَايْمًا. Both are correct and equally common.
Putting it first adds a little emphasis on the time, just like "every day I study" compared with "I study every day".
⚠️ One thing isn't flexible: عَم must sit **directly** in front of its verb, with nothing in between.

blocks.text: Notice the verbs with a long vowel in the middle of the stem — رَاح، شَاف، نَام — whose "you" and "he" forms use بِتْـ and بِيـ, not بْتِـ and بْيِـ. This small difference comes from the sound, not from a rule you need to memorize; repeating the table aloud is enough.

blocks.title: The verb بْحِبّ and its two meanings
items: Followed by a noun, it means **like** or **love**: بْحِبّ الْقَهْوِة ("I like coffee").
Followed by a bare verb, it means **like doing**: بْحِبّ إِمْشِي ("I like walking").
⚠️ To say "I want", use بَدِّي from unit 7, not بْحِبّ. The sentence بْحِبّ إِشْرَب قَهْوِة means "I like drinking coffee", not "I want to drink coffee now".

exercises.prompt: Change to the form asked for.
Fill in عَم, or leave the gap empty, depending on the meaning.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: عَم بِدْرُس. — كِلّ يَوْم بِشْرَب قَهْوِة. — عَم بْتِسْتَنَّى الْبَاص. — مَا مْنِشْتِغِل الْيَوْم. — مَا بْتِرْكَب بَاص أَبَدًا؟ — عَم بْيَاكْلُوا.
مْنِدْرُس — بْيِشْتِغْلُوا — بْتِشْرْبِي — بْتَاكُل — بِتْرُوحُوا — بِيحِبّ
عَم بِدْرُس بِالْمَكْتَبِة. — كِلّ يَوْم بِشْرَب قَهْوِة. — مَا بِشْتِغِل الْيَوْم. — شُو عَم تَعْمْلِي؟ — دَايْمًا بْيِرْجَعُوا بَكِّير. — مَا بِرْكَب بَاص أَبَدًا.
wave: Tell yourself about today in five sentences: three with عَم for what's happening now, two without عَم for your habits.
